title: Business Model Generation
source_note: Book itself not read. Facts come from Wikipedia (Business Model Canvas), Strategyzer, a Shortform summary and publisher listings. The Wikipedia page for the book returned 404.

facts.claim: The book Business Model Generation (Osterwalder, Pigneur, with Tim Clark credited on Wikipedia) appeared in 2010; the publisher says it was co-created by 470 practitioners from 45 countries.
facts.source: Wikipedia Business Model Canvas; Wiley listing

facts.claim: Osterwalder proposed the nine building blocks in 2005, from PhD work on business model ontology supervised by Yves Pigneur; the thesis is dated 2004.
The nine blocks: customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partners, cost structure.
The canvas is printed on a large surface so groups can sketch and discuss the blocks with sticky notes or board markers.
Layout: the right side represents the market, the left side what it takes to serve that market, with value propositions between them.
The blocks are interdependent: changing a customer segment affects channels, activities and costs; a change in one block can constrain or amplify the others.
Criticism: the canvas is static (does not capture how a model evolves), says little about how components interact, and is conceptually isolated from the environment.
Patterns chapter covers unbundling, the long tail, multi-sided platforms, FREE as a business model, and open business models.

Free pattern: at least one customer group always gets value for free, financed by another part of the model or another segment. Three subtypes: advertising, freemium (premium services), bait and hook (continuing purchases).
Advertising subtype: Google is the summary's example; advertiser revenue enables users to search for free. Facebook also discussed.
Multi-sided platform: two or more interdependent customer groups; the more active users a platform attracts, the more value it offers both sides.
Bait and hook examples in the summary: coffee machines that need capsules, printers that need ink. A reversal also exists: a high-priced premium product with a low-priced complement.
Revenue stream types listed for the canvas: asset sale, usage fee, subscription, lending/leasing/renting, licensing, brokerage, advertising.
A business model describes how an organization creates, delivers and captures value (the book's own definition, recalled, not re-verified).
